findings.title: New installations bypass the GitHub installer identity check
findings.body: When there is no existing `Integration` row for the supplied installation ID, this branch immediately advances the pipeline without comparing the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user to the app installation sender. The integration is then created from the installation ID in a later pipeline step. Consequently, a Sentry organization administrator who knows or obtains another GitHub App installation ID can authorize with their own GitHub account and attach an installation that has not yet been recorded by Sentry (for example before its webhook is processed) to their Sentry organization, potentially gaining Sentry-mediated access to that installation's repositories. The validation must also be enforced for the first creation of an integration, using a trustworthy installer identity rather than only existing webhook-backed records.

findings.title: Legacy or pipeline-created integrations without sender metadata cause a 500
findings.body: The comparison indexes `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` unconditionally. Integrations created by the normal pipeline do not populate `sender` in `build_integration`, and integrations created before this change also lack it (the updated basic-flow test still asserts metadata without `sender`). If such an active integration remains after its OrganizationIntegration is removed and is installed again, this path raises `KeyError` instead of returning the installation failure response. Handle absent sender metadata explicitly and provide a safe validation/migration path.

findings.title: OAuth transport and user-info failures escape as server errors
findings.body: Only parsing the access-token response is guarded. `safe_urlopen` can raise for a GitHub/network HTTP failure, and `get_user_info` can raise when the returned token is rejected or the user API is unavailable. Either exception escapes the pipeline and returns a 500 rather than the intended invalid-installation response. Catch the expected HTTP/API exceptions around both the token exchange and user lookup and return `error(...)` so invalid, reused, or failed OAuth codes fail safely as described.
